deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous German prose note on the political history of Macedonia in the Diadochi period (c. 286–278 BC). It continues the previous page (Cassander's successors and Demetrius Poliorcetes) and runs into the next page (the Gauls at Delphi, Antigonus Gonatas, Pyrrhus, and a king list). It reads like lecture or reading notes in universal history; the hand and content give no sign of Gauss's own mathematical work. Paraphrase in order:

(1) 286: Demetrius Poliorcetes is surrounded by Seleucus' troops; he dies (†) 284.

(2) Lysimachus and Pyrrhus both aim at the Macedonian throne. In 287 Pyrrhus obtains it and afterwards gives (verb omitted in the MS) part of Macedonia to Lysimachus. In 286 Pyrrhus has to evacuate Macedonia again.

(3) Lysimachus becomes king and unites Thrace with Macedonia. He dies (†) 282 in a war against Seleucus Nicator (the battle of Corupedium, not named in the text).

(4) Seleucus now wants to become 'general master' (ruler of all). In 281 he is killed in Europe by Ptolemaeus Ceraunus. Ceraunus takes his treasures and becomes master of Macedonia, and he murders the remaining sons of Lysimachus.

(5) In 279 Ceraunus is killed by the Gauls. Macedonia is in the greatest danger. Meleager and Antipater are made king in turn but deposed just as quickly.

(6) Sosthenes takes command and beats the Gauls. In 278 the Gauls return in greater numbers; Sosthenes resists, is defeated and killed. The next page continues with the Gauls reaching Delphi.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: Historical dating (by modern chronology): Demetrius Poliorcetes surrendered to Seleucus in 285 and died in 283 BC. The MS has 286 and †284; older chronologies sometimes give 284.
Pyrrhus and Lysimachus jointly took Macedonia in 288/287. Pyrrhus was expelled by Lysimachus in 285/284, not 286.
Lysimachus fell at Corupedium in 281 BC; the MS gives 282, a date also found in some older handbooks.
The large Gallic invasion under Brennus that reached Delphi is usually dated 279 BC; the MS gives 278. Sosthenes' resistance is dated 279–277 in modern accounts.
Grammatical omission: in 'der hernach dem Lysimachus einen Theil von Macedonien' the verb is missing (e.g. 'abtrat' or 'überlassen musste').
Ptolemy Ceraunus killed the young sons of Lysimachus by Arsinoe. The MS wording ('the remaining descendants of Lysimachus') is a loose but acceptable summary.

results.what: Historical summary of Macedonian succession 286–278 BC: Demetrius, Pyrrhus, Lysimachus, Seleucus, Ptolemy Ceraunus, Meleager, Antipater Etesias, Sosthenes, and the Gallic invasion
results.modern_name: Diadochi / early Hellenistic Macedonian history (standard textbook material)
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient sources (Justin, Pausanias, Plutarch, Diodorus), as compiled in 18th/19th-century universal-history textbooks

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical: routine school or lecture notes on ancient Macedonian history with conventional (partly older) dates. It contains no mathematical content of any kind. Whether the hand is even Gauss's is doubtful.

checkable.asserts: Ceraunus ruled about 2 years: from Seleucus' death (281 BC) to his own death at the hands of the Gauls (279 BC). This is a trivial internal consistency check of the dates on the page.
In the MS chronology Pyrrhus held the Macedonian throne about one year (287 to 286 BC). This is an internal consistency check only.

transcription_corrections: Line 1–2: 'ein geschlossen' should be read as one word, 'eingeschlossen'.
'Trohn' appears to be the writer's own spelling (= Thron); retain it with [sic] rather than correct it.
'der her nach dem Lysimachus' is better read 'der hernach dem Lysimachus …'; a verb such as 'abtrat' is missing in the MS itself.
'Etwaigen[?] Nachkommen[?] vom Lysimachus übrig' is more likely 'Einige[?] noch Söhne[?] vom Lysimachus übrig'. Ceraunus murdered Lysimachus' sons, which supports 'Söhne'.
'Antipater[?]': the MS form looks like 'Antipater'/'Artipater'. Historically this is Antipater Etesias, so 'Antipater' is correct.
'Sos. wider setzte sich' should be read 'Sos[thenes] widersetzte sich', split across the line break.
